Historically, a depth-probe DNA microarray was used to assess the extent of a complex across multiple loci. However, the practicalities of a deep probe to multiple loci, such as the overlap between individual sequencing platforms, can limit the utility of such methods. Several recent reports have shown that individual multi-target platforms can be aggregated to form broader approaches for in-tissue quantification of gene interactions, including multiple complexes, transcripts, proteins, or RNAs. Here, we combine the single-plate read-out of newly developed multicolor and quadruplex approaches to micro-array image stacks with the mass spectrometric quantification capabilities of the Oxford Nanopore MinION system. Specifically, we applied this method to quantitative analysis of individual complexes using the Assay of Intended Recombination Multiplexed Sequence Analysis (AIMS), a multi-array based on acoustic wave propagation to interrogate nucleic acid interaction regions. AIMS is capable of simultaneously imaging several targets interacting with each other through single-nucleotide sequences. Taking advantage of the compact architecture of the Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencer, we were able to simultaneously quantify the interactions between four transcriptional regulators on five different target genes, each imprinted on two different locations. In 500 bp genomic fragments spanning the non-coding sequences of two genes, in excess of one transcript, and spanning two expression levels for two transcription factor (TF) targets, the average gene-to-gene interaction strength was estimated to be 11-100 Kb on average, with clustering coefficient around 0.5. This approach could be extended to other microscope-based platforms using acoustic wave propagation, such as the ever-popular iTSSEQ instrument from Bolt Biosciences. In addition, we note that the spatial and temporal resolution of the Detectorless Transmembrane Acoustic Sensing (DTAS) multiplexers is sufficient to quantify the interactions between multiple targets.

Genome-scale models are a promising way to study human protein function. However, few comprehensive studies have been conducted to characterize experimentally validated genomes of pseudogene families. Here, we developed from scratch COSMIC (a functional genomic analysis tool for gene-specific pseudogene datasets), a method to integrate experimentally validated (nascent/exon-free) pseudogene datasets into computationally generated genome-scale models with experimentally determined protein sequences. In COSMIC we have generated five datasets from the GROSAMAT custom analysis of pseudogene families and compiled publicly available publicly available evidence-based gene sequences for the development of these models. COSMIC can be used as an experimental tool for the exploration of the hypothesis of complete gene loss in DNA repair genes, yeast pseudogenes, and all classes of cytosine-rich pseudogenes. We have used COSMIC to explore two independently produced pseudogene datasets for CRISPR-Cas9-modified protein editing. The potential impact of CRISPR-Cas9 on computational versions of pseudogene data sets is discussed. In this study we used the COSMIC evaluation tool to investigate how this new tool could be improved.

There is substantial evidence supporting the chromosome 10 variants that produce DiGeorge syndrome as causal for microcephaly. Most of these studies use signal transduction (SM) assays to study these variant's impact on embryonic gene expression. However, such approaches can be limited due to a lack of prognostic biological information. To assess these microcephaly-causing variation's effect on systemic gene expression and phenotypic outcomes, we used a BAX inhibitor cell line under high dose treatment with the canonical causative variant, ζ10-R1880C, to explore how it influences these key skeletal mesoderm-related genes that define the cryptoglossum complex. We also investigated how this case-infected cell line would respond to four other variant-induced chromosomal rearrangements to assess its transcriptional and functional signature during progression to CNS. We found highly reduced BAX expression in the CNS before and after intracellular Ca2+ treatments. We also identified high and low penetrance versions of the four disruption variants in the host of the heterozygous case variant. Still, the most prevalent damage variant (αT1880G) had extremely low penetrance. Furthermore, we found that the combination of three of these variants (αT1880G, γ10-R1880C, and αT1880L) could explain 87% of the observed CpG region damage, but only one of the four variants that was predominantly pathogenic was able to account for the lowest penetrance version. The combination of several variants had an equal incidence of CNS damage across the model. The variant most closely related to the phenotype was associated with low penetrance of these variants and an exclusive CNS damage phenotype of IBD-258. To compare the characterization of variant-affected BAX with that observed in other tissues and systems, we performed an informal experimental analysis by identifying 1087 BAXs from BAX locus cells or their mutant counterparts across all BAX-suppressing drug classes on the NT-Pro-P platform. Oligonucleotide short palindromic repeats (OligoPreds) constitute a small class of repetitive short tandem repeat (STR) motifs present in the human genome that control transcription. This class of repeats can be recognised by oligonucleotide array analysis of genomic DNA or other short DNA sequences and therefore are ideal input for single-cell interrogation to predict their presence. The occurrence of predicted SSR repeats and key gene signatures in patients is relevant for drug target development, but incomplete knowledge of genomes exposes the challenge of determining specificity and prevalence using standard reverse phase shotgun sequencing methods alone. Next-generation sequencing based single-cell screening technologies, including closed-tube single cell-genome-wide sequencing (cSTSGS) combined with mRNA analysis, recently emerged as a promising approach to develop one-step, whole-cell-based measurement approaches to interrogate cell function with high sensitivity and accuracy. Here, we propose to exploit the complementary strengths of next-generation sequencing to assess SSR and genomics signatures in small numbers of immune cells without the time-consuming, laborious and potentially costly bioprocessing steps that are necessary when analysing live cells at high cellular resolution. Using cSTSGS we demonstrate that myeloma cells accumulate features linked to chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) with multiple well-established diseases and a multitude of potential targets. We conclude that combining cSTSGS technologies can be used to evaluate the presence of specific novel selective mutagen species, accelerate the evaluation of Sanger library-only and cSTSGS-based genome screening and provide the means to assess key signatures using whole cell-based systems.

Species-specific alterations in gene expression occur naturally as well as artificially through gene editing of genetic materials, allowing for the genetic-based treatment of disorders and other health challenges. While synthetic genomics advances hold great promise for improving biomedical research and interventions, there are significant hurdles, including limited access to genetic sequencing and editing platforms and difficulty and limited availability of parts of the necessary plasmids. We have developed a platform that allows generic plasmids for molecular engineering of any desired target gene. The technology we have developed follows a standard common-sensical approach that uses plasmid-free sequencing technology from UniGene, followed by the generation of purification and termination vectors using a rapid single-base-pair technology for NGene-seq (NGeneSeq). Duplications in the human genome have caused significant variability across populations and genetic regions in genetic studies. Cancers arise from genomic alterations, including homologous recombination-associated genomic instability and tandem repeat expansion, caused by the duplication of the DNA. Here, we describe an approach of constructing synthetic human genomic DNA using overlapping tri-nucleotide repeats and the creation of short tandem repeats (STR) and base modification-specific regions (BSRs). Synthetic DNA allows single nucleotide variants, insertions, deletions, and other types of gene mutations without the issues of naturally occurring DNA mutations. The chimeric-like sequences were developed to investigate structural features, plasmid functionality and RE fusion with short tandem repeats (STRs). We fused trinary genes (3r) with STRs from four different constructs (A to D). The cells fused with other constructs from 3r-A, 3r-B, 3r-C and 3r-D did not exhibit significant immune response after transplantation into a syngeneic host, T-cell leukemia, NK cell leukemia, in vitro studies. The four-fortified construct AD104 contained 12 constructs in 4 molecules, with 25 various-generation repeats and a repeating pattern of 6 different repeats. It allowed scientists to investigate the phenotypic variability of different human genome integrations in cells.

Human mitochondrial transplantation has the potential to cure rare diseases due to mitochondrial DNA defects. Introducing transgenic mitochondria into the nucleus of adult somatic cells holds therapeutic promise for restoring mitochondrial function and could eventually increase the survival of mitochondria derived from adult somatic cells. Here, we introduce a genome editing approach that uses C[>∼]NSOuppy CRISPR/Cas9 nucleases and TlMr.Green to improve (ChlB) intermediate filament gene expression by introducing a C[>∼] to replace exons 10-12 of (ChlB), resulting in 80% increase in (ChlB) production. After transgenics of adult iPS cells were introduced in the hematopoietic niche of mice, the mice were treated with a low dose of (ChlB) with the total dose of (ChlB) 30 fold higher than (ChlB), demonstrating that our CRISPRi approach leads to a dose-dependent increase of expression of (ChlB) in hematopoietic niches. As a novel treatment approach for difficult-to-cure mitochondrial diseases, we anticipate that our work may advance the clinical application of restoring mitochondrial function by implanting genetically modified iPSCs.

#RNA FISH is a powerful molecular biology tool widely used to characterize the transcriptome in various tissues and diseases, in particular the human brain. This technology also offers the possibility to directly monitor and compare RNA in situ during cell differentiation, because it has been used to determine RNA processing at different developmental stages. However, until recently, no technology existed to image and quantify cell differentiation with this advanced functional technology.

AimsTo overcome this issue, we have designed cell-specific probes that exploit distinct mRNA signals during cell differentiation for both fluorescence (phospho-specific) and UV/visible (RNF-specific) labels.

MethodsTwo universal cell-specific probes to cell differentiation were developed, which are generated by a biohybrid fluorescence probe based on site-specific recombination and a corresponding RNA-binding aptamer. The specificity and sensitivity of the cell-specific probes were evaluated through two in vitro (cells at diverse developmental stages) and in vivo (mice) experiments.

ResultsF, acta-14.50-14.50T11-21-14.50-15.55, ssG8-32, and auto-sIP6 were successfully validated, with a ~95% cross-reactivity between the fluorescent probes and target proteins.

ConclusionWe developed an RNA FISH technology based on fixed-point and domain-based multi-protein interactions, and we have successfully developed and applied cell-specific probes for the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells and neural progenitor cells. The utility and robustness of this technology can be applied to further investigate the molecular mechanisms of cell differentiation and improve understanding of brain development in diseases such as autism.

Splicing is critical for the translational regulation of gene expression within genomes. Splicing often requires the recruitment of a single spliceosome isoform [1], and multiple copies of this same isoform can interfere with a spliceosome complex. We report that depletion of the fission yeast Sfo1 requires human splicing by humans Dva53, and that Dva53 is associated with reduced protein expression and human dysfunction. We demonstrate that an engineered variant of Dva53, specifically engineered to express the isoform associated with human splicing, rescues Dva53-associated phenotypes. Genetic studies of several Sfo1 mutants reveal that these mutator genes are regulated by quorum-dependent regulation of Dva53. Expression of individual clones of the Dva53-associated isoform rescued mRNA levels in these mutants, and individual clones of a human spliceosome gene rescued mRNA levels from mutagenic De<u>VA</u>53 in these mutants. Consistent with this phenotype, silencing of the human Sfo1 gene in either the Somatic Stem Cell (SSC) or lymphocyte progenitors (HL) with radiation rescue the SOS1 spliceosomal protein. The ssof1-/- SSC and Lymphoblastoid Cell Line (LCL)-hSsf1-/- HL worms only develop infertility defects, and together rescue the phenotypes of these cells. Both the ssf1-/- SSC and the Sfo1-/- SSC display protective phenotypes of reduced germ line proliferation and increased susceptibility to gonadal atrophy. Together, these findings reveal that splicing as the first and most predominant epigenetic modification is critical for the maintenance of germ cell numbers.

Mitochondrial division occurs during cellular differentiation in both yeast and human cells. When given the choice of one or both maternal progenitors, a gene might choose to upregulate one of these markers: the elongation factor 2A (eEF2A) that is enriched in the maternal progenitor that passes it, or the elongation factor 2B (eEF2B) that is enriched in the paternal progenitor that functions downstream of the gene. We have developed the mitotic proliferation prediction (MPP) software to allow researchers to consider how to best predict whether a gene has a paternal or maternal target sequence. Here we extend the MPP-XENR model to incorporate the biophysical parameters associated with those particles, as the genes have varying conformations within a particle, and thus are affected by such thermodynamic parameters. We find that although MPP can be highly accurate for genes of either biological sex, only the maternal-only RNA is enriched in 1682 kinases according to genome-scale protein engineering studies using only human chromosomes. This is because an internal alpha helical domain is not observed in the male-specific-enriched 1682 kinases. The maternal and paternal isoform of the 1682 kinase, ONF1-BP2, is driven by male-specific-enriched motifs with opposite amino acid polarity and is enriched in all target sequences, and this role is seen for 1678 members of the 1682 kinases. We present MPP for predictions of unbiased gene cluster genes only, which are not subject to primary bias, and which include also biases from genes that do not have an eEF2A and eEF2B duplication within the cluster. We further offer free MPP software and analysis, including a website with its tutorial.
sample_p_texts: We demonstrate here the use of optical genome mapping (OGM) to detect genetic alterations arising from gene editing by various technologies in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). OGM enables an unbiased and comprehensive analysis of the entire genome, allowing the detection of genomic structural variants (SVs) of all classes with a quantitative variant allele frequency (VAF) sensitivity of 5%. In this pilot study, we conducted a comparative dual analysis between the parental iPSCs and the derived cells that had undergone gene editing using various techniques, including transposons, lentiviral transduction, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated safe harbor locus insertion at the adeno-associated virus integration site 1 (AAVS1). These analyses demonstrated that iPSCs that had been edited using transposons or lentiviral transduction resulted in a high number of transgene insertions in the genome. In contrast, CRISPR-Cas9 technology resulted in a more precise and limited transgene insertion, with only a single target sequence observed at the intended locus. These studies demonstrate the value of OGM to detect genetic alterations in engineered cell products and suggests that OGM, together with DNA sequencing, could be a valuable tool when evaluating genetically modified iPSCs for research and therapeutic purposes.

Investigating chromosomal instability and aneuploidy within tumors is essential for understanding tumorigenesis and developing diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Single-cell DNA sequencing technologies have enabled such analyses, revealing aneuploidies specific to individual cells within the same tumor. However, it has been difficult to scale the throughput of these methods to detect rare aneuploidies while maintaining high sensitivity. To overcome this deficit, we developed KaryoTap, a method combining custom targeted DNA sequencing panels for the Tapestri platform with a computational framework to enable detection of chromosome- and chromosome arm-scale aneuploidy (gains or losses) and copy number neutral loss of heterozygosity in all human chromosomes across thousands of single cells simultaneously. KaryoTap allows detecting gains and losses with an average accuracy of 83% for arm events and 91% for chromosome events. Importantly, together with chromosomal copy number, our system allows us to detect barcodes and gRNAs integrated into the cells genome, thus enabling pooled CRISPR- or ORF-based functional screens in single cells. As a proof of principle, we performed a small screen to expand the chromosomes that can be targeted by our recently described CRISPR-based KaryoCreate system for engineering aneuploidy in human cells. KaryoTap will prove a powerful and flexible approach for the study of aneuploidy and chromosomal instability in both tumors and normal tissues.

As with most enzyme-storage disorders, DNA testing at an early age is critical for identifying genetic variants and their impact on disease burden. Still, most variants in genes such as Iduronate-2-sulfatase, IDS, are Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS). In patients presenting with Hunter Syndrome, clinical testing for IDS enzyme activity has been the mainstay to determine whether a variant is likely damaging. However, these enzyme assays are unable to predict disease severity or neuronal toxicity and may be missing many aspects of IDS pathology. In this study, we have developed an image-based assay using genome-engineered cells with IDS mutations to identify if a specific mutation causes lysosomal and membrane disruptions that characterize the disease. Specifically, we generate twelve mutant cell lines and document both the biochemical changes in IDS activity and the reproducible phenotypic differences therein. Next, we examine two patient-derived cell lines and find the same phenotypic differences in these lines compared to parental controls. The phenotypic changes are measured on a specific scale, which we term the PathScoreLC. To determine whether the observed changes are specific to IDS, we reintroduce a recombinant version of the IDS enzyme (rhIDS) to rescue both the biochemical and phenotypic changes of these cells. Interestingly, even after 120 hours, rescue is present, but not all the cells return to normal, which may also reflect the pathological state. Finally, we examine the gene expression differences and find that recombinant enzyme is not sufficient to induce transcriptional changes in the mutant lines at the time points studied. Overall, these cell-based lysosomal and membrane phenotypes may be key to quickly and accurately profiling clinical variants in the IDS gene.

In earlier studies, we optimized an assay system for the genome-wide detection of copy number variation (CNV) in diploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells, based on selection for formaldehyde plus copper (FA+Cu) resistance conferred by the amplification of a dosage-dependent reporter cassette, SFA1-CUP1. Our analyses identified a robust bias for terminal deletions of the right arm of Chr7 (Chr7R) associated with unbalanced translocations. This bias was observed at approximately constant strength across all three sites where the amplification reporter cassette was inserted, in CNV-carrying yeast clones derived both spontaneously and from mutagen-induced recombinogenic conditions. We conducted allelic mitotic recombination experiments to investigate the possibility of the presence of a fragile site on Chr7R, but the results disfavored this model, and instead indicated that the Chr7R bias applies only to non-allelic rearrangements. We validated the existence of a CNV formation bias at Chr7R through an orthologous NAHR competition approach that was independent of selection for FA+Cu resistance. Finally, we showed the in contrast to its high participation in NAHR as a recipient sequence, Chr7R becomes amplified as a translocation donor less frequently than other comparable regions of the genome. To begin unraveling the cause of this unusual behavior, we evaluated the effect of a set of candidate genes involved in chromatin mobility and sister chromatid cohesion on the rearrangement spectra involving Chr7R. We found that deletion mutations in some of these genes, particularly SAP30, attenuated the biased NAHR behavior. Taken together, our results suggested that although Chr7R is not inherently more prone to DNA breakage than other regions, once a DNA lesion is formed there, it has a higher propensity to undergo inappropriate repair leading to a chromosomal rearrangement.

Pathogenic variants in MECP2 commonly lead to Rett syndrome, where MECP2s function as a DNA cytosine methylation reader is believed critical. MECP2 variants are also catalogued in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), including nine missense variants which had no known clinical significance at the start of this study. To assess these nine variants as risk alleles for ASD, we developed MECP2 variant functional assays using budding yeast and Drosophila. We calibrated these assays with known pathogenic and benign variants. Our data predict that four ASD variants are loss of function and five are functional. Protein destabilization offers insight into the altered function of some of these variants. Notably, yeast and Drosophila lack DNA methylation, yet all Rett pathogenic and ASD variants located in the methyl DNA binding domain that we analyzed proved to be loss of function, suggesting a clinically-relevant role for non-methyl DNA-binding by MECP2.

Amino-terminal (Nt-) acetylation (NTA) is a common protein modification, affecting 80% of cytosolic proteins in humans. The human essential gene, NAA10, encodes the enzyme NAA10, as the catalytic subunit for the N-terminal acetyltransferase A (NatA) complex, including the accessory protein, NAA15. The first human disease directly involving NAA10 was discovered in 2011, and it was named Ogden syndrome (OS), after the location of the first affected family residing in Ogden, Utah, USA. Since that time, other variants have been found in NAA10 and NAA15. Here we describe the generation of 31 iPSC lines, with 16 from females and 15 from males. This cohort includes CRISPR-mediated correction to the wild-type genotype in 4 male lines, along with editing one female line to generate homozygous wild-type or mutant clones. Following the monoclonalizaiton and screening for X-chromosome activation status in female lines, 3 additional pairs of female lines, in which either the wild type allele is on the active X chromosome (Xa) or the pathogenic variant allele is on Xa, have been generated. Subsets of this cohort have been successfully used to make cardiomyocytes and neural progenitor cells (NPCs). These cell lines are made available to the community via the NYSCF Repository.

Function-specific expression patterns of genes and microRNAs (miRNAs) reveal the genetic and epigenetic mechanisms underlying diseases. However, existing bioinformatics tools can only identify genes and miRNA pathways based on de-orphanization of all genes. To address this challenge, we established a novel algorithm, called deorphan_disease (DoD) that operates as a disease enrichment tool to discover enrichment modules for the interaction between gene expression and disease state, with independent modules tuned for differential responses. This approach can distinguish gene expression and miRNA signatures in gene interaction patterns with a super-fractional size distribution (10s/number of genes). We use our method to provide disease-specific functional insights for pre-established and newly-discovered disease pathways. Our novel description, and analysis and comparison of pathogenicity, efficacy, and functional relevance of these disease-derived interactions, is based on our in silico dataset. Using DoD, we identified miRNAs and genes critical for developmental and genetic processes that influence disease risk and treatment response. We demonstrate the power of DoD to predict various clinical diagnosis and management issues, from fragile X syndrome to autism spectrum disorders, with a top 1-categorical diagnosis for 185 of our 175 genes from 78 biological pathways. Our results highlight the utility of DoD to reveal biological insights from public databases for novel gene-disease interaction patterns. DoD enabled us to discover differential responses of gene clusters from drug sensitivity to sensitivity. DoD enables identifying disease-related relevant and actionable interaction combinations. DoD also highlights the weakness of using such data to reach a clinical precision diagnosis. As a proof of concept, we applied this method to predict AML risk in an ESRI clinical data-set that contains 1140 genes, 4 disease groups, 56 adverse events and 5 common databases for discovery of AML risk factors, and found a cancer-specific gene group was absent from all databases, demonstrating the weaknesses of using such data for risk prediction and evidence for adverse-event causality.
