Drug discovery in infectious disease is challenging due to the impact of mutations across genetic background across pathogenic microbial species. Generative Chemistry (GC) is a growing area of translational disease prediction. In this study, we applied GC to develop a single gene-specific predictor that can identify druggable targets with higher accuracy and lower false-positive rates compared to traditional scoring functions.

Results: Our GC model, incorporating gene history and biopharma using both pre-mRNA and post-transcriptional start sites, achieved a hit rate of 7.92% and 6.14% for specific biomarkers. Notably, our GC model substantially improved the model accuracy on base-phenotyping data (from 12.2% to 18.5%), a critical aspect for improving the performance of diverse, polymorphic host genome-guided pharmacogenomic predictions. We further observed a remarkable improvement in model accuracy when using the expression of the target sequence rather than known reference markers (from 37.4% to 74.2% and 9.6% to 22.5%), reflecting the broader application of GC as an alternative to estimating in-house drug-like or drug-like mutations (LI, DtLc).

Impact: Our GC-based model offers a more accurate, unbiased, and universal drug-like target predictor. The LI<sub>G), a parameter of the model hyperparameter, can be replaced with the K-NEA-derived mRNA base mapping and expression data in our application to pre-mRNA and post-transcriptional start sites. It is not required to have all genes and genes at all transition points in the genome and all genes at all variant intervals.

The advancement of whole exome sequencing technologies has revolutionised medical diagnostics, allowing for the identification of rare Mendelian conditions, solid tumours, and other diseases. One example is the development of ReliaSeq by Harvard University, which uses deep learning to identify the expanded disease states in specific genes. An alternative approach called CBOmics has been proposed and recently shown high sensitivity for detecting disease states. Furthermore, the presence of vast changes in known disease states, rare diseases, and normalisation effects, indicates the need for wide-ranging clinical testing in the clinical setting. Here, we present CBRun, a software tool designed for future biomarker discovery and evaluation in a large population using the DAISY cohort, a national health database of approximately 40 million people. CBRun combines a real-world clinical research approach to an AI method to identify probable Mendelian disease state, cancer, and uncommon rare variants. CBRun uses gene annotations, genetic clinical information, and genotype data from the DAISY cohort to map each disease state to a biological concept, quantify the contribution of each identified disease state in total potential genetic risk (TPGR) in the whole population, and the impact on the population at-risk. CBRun can also generate biological concepts to capture the other contributions of contributing variants, random model effects, and integrated hit probabilities. CBRun can be applied to other genomics and medical informatics data modalities. It can also be applied to future uses of deep learning and AI.

The growing global prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) is not only translating into the development of multiple interventions but also demand for novel computational approaches to provide reliable and easy-to-interpret predictions. The availability of large, generalizable, clinical datasets is a crucial factor for successful efforts to improve new treatments. Here we propose state-of-the-art public datasets for diabetes prediction, including recent publicly available phenotypes and traits data. Notably, the datasets we introduce cover over 90% of predicted phenotypes from CDR1 and CDR2 built using modern machine learning algorithms across all human tissues from 40 diseases and 136 000 subjects. We also introduce a novel methodology that automatically calculates the most meaningful training samples in each dataset, preparing optimal samples for supervised prediction. Altogether, these resources enable impactful analysis of real data from public datasets with state-of-the-art computational algorithms to determine genomic regions associated with T2D. Results from the T2D genomic coordinates, classification algorithms, and analysis tools are publicly available at bd3diabetes.org.

The Human Genome Genotype 10K and ENCODE (Ensembl gene-annotation-quality data) data are one of the biggest and most comprehensive datasets worldwide, revealing both high accuracy for individual gene annotation and sequencing coverage, which enables high throughput annotation quality measures such as GG ratio. There has been ongoing interest in leveraging annotated transcripts to quantify the complexity of complex human pathways. While transcriptomics can measure a plethora of interactions between genes, data curation and manual transcript annotation remain a manual effort. In this paper, we propose an approach for automatic transcript mapping based on second order tensors, integrating MEDev ecosystem to assist with curation. Our approach exploits deep learning models to score enriched modules and apply probabilistic explanation matching to quantify the interactions between associated genes. We demonstrate that our approach (Truemake) is able to automate the creation of gene paths and score enrichment based on the underlying deep network, without the need for annotation manual curation.

Significance statementUsing a publicly available protein interaction dataset from Deep Path Analytics, we address the challenges of genome-scale transcriptomics. We show that automation of curation is possible by using biologically plausible, personalized, and context-dependent ontology categories. We apply our platform, Truemake, for the first time to predict exon-intron interactions and quantify the depth of bulk-subcellular interactions.

Identifying causes of disease with high precision remains a significant research area in system biology and public health. Here, we introduce "The Rare Causes Database (T-RCD)", an integrated and machine-learning based data exploration framework for pathogen-associated genetic variants (PAGs), a spectrum of genetic and epigenomic data spanning the entire genome of humans, patients, and 27 rare human diseases. Starting with global association statistics derived from GWAS studies of the entire human genome (based on three diverse human samples, 60,418 candidate alleles, and 431,606 probeset variants), we iteratively build the T-RCD with an ontology-agnostic representation of disease phenotypes from six disease-specific domains. We then use T-RCD to uncover novel and rare causes of human diseases and their rare subpopulations, achieving state-of-the-art recall, precision, and precision at risk.

Results match the average findings from current large genomic databases such as HapMap, Genomes 2001, ClinXome, and MetaSPaRC, and offer a fast approach to epidemiological inference of rare genetic-epigenomic processes in both medical and biomedical sciences. In the following parts, we demonstrate that T-RCD effectively leverages samples of genetic and epigenomic features of clinical datasets to uncover the highly polymorphic genetic variants for a wide spectrum of rare conditions, and present exemplary models of multivariable models for each rare cause, paving the way to comprehensive and long-lasting open science infrastructures.

Missense, nonsense, and exonic truncation variants impact large-scale networks, but the consequences of genetic variants have long been a challenge in computational biology. In silico GWAS show conflicting results. By predicting possible functional consequences of mutations in all proteins, we show that all regions can be generalized to all proteins, whereas the accuracy of single protein protein annotations is highly context-dependent. We also show that a decrease in low-frequency alleles can greatly impact the accuracy of this disease detection pipeline, especially when focusing on protein subnetworks.

MethodsWe combined two high-performance high-throughput networks: the high-resolution soluble network and the transcribed low-resolution protein network (StrainTre) with an ensemble that models brain-targeted, but yet-to-be classified SNVs. We experimentally address a single SNV by investigating if the specificity of the attached network improves during testing. We used a widely adopted, accurate off-the-shelf SNV, but trained the training set accordingly so it is representative of future variants. We predicted the effects of one SNV, identify subnetworks, and experimentally test whether SNVs depend on known networks or novel domains in the same way as recently proposed SNVs. Our best-performing model achieved an 85.48 mean precision (85.60 specificity) in the deep brain region, confirming network dependencies and prior predictions. This surpasses the 82.41 mean precision across Deep Brain Networks with known domain interactions. In addition, we demonstrate that the OnSmoker GWAS prediction algorithm: is computationally resource-efficient and unbiased with respect to the specifics of the SNV variants and their target networks. Our study underlines the role of subnetworks and networks in the prediction of proteins and genes and is a novel approach to biomedical variants.

HighlightsMachine learning revealed functional consequences of single mutations across large-scale networks, but proteins usually have very few functional annotations.

BackgroundThere are millions of children with spina bifida (SB) worldwide. Standardized diagnostic methods like scannograms are reliable but are labor intensive and battery of standard tests are not practical for routine clinical use. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more accurate and less invasive, but still requires experienced radiologists to perform an entire examination, with MRI markers and volume calculations, which adds to the labor. Advances in machine learning in recent years could help alleviate the burden of standard clinical tests, and as a result, a growing body of literature shows a variety of machine learning models for spina bifida diagnosis using CT data. However, prior machine learning methods have been developed in specific disease conditions, and clinical study data may differ, leading to heterogeneous and inconsistent results.

MethodsHere we applied AlphaFold2 and TwinVRX models to three machine learning classification models for ab initio detection of SB. AlphaFold2 uses a non-local molecular dynamic simulator to evaluate spina bifida gene interactions, as most SB cases are caused by single gene mutations. On the other hand, the TwinVRX model simulates brain ventricle dynamics and is also based on gene interaction predictions. It was trained on a set of morphologically informative CT markers in pairs and was developed to infer spina bifida disease-related global functional features. We tested these models against two external datasets: one containing thousands of symptom-free scans, representative for spina bifida asymptomatic state, which has been used previously for the teaching and training of AI-based decision tools, and the second using French eHeartCT dataset to explore risk of spina bifida in the population. We evaluated performance by intersectional and crossover comparisons between the 2 models and comparison to standard radiologists using HoldOut method and the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve. As a double-blind study was not possible, we also compared model performance in a blinded manner by using a concept drift test performed using the same algorithm for patient samples in the dataset.

ResultsIn total, 7601 SB and 518 healthy patients were included for evaluation of model performance. In 913 lesions on CT images, AlphaFold 2 showed higher accuracy (AUC) of 98.29% in distinguishing patients with SB (vs 97.61% for CT). TwinVRX demonstrated a higher diagnostic sensitivity (AUC = 81.42) compared to AlphaFold. The differences were apparent in the ROC curve. A model that predicts a greater percentage of cases in normal,

Variations in microRNA (miRNA) expression can be heritable, complex diseases are governed by multiple biological/environmental inputs, and disease risk assessments often conflate these components. Here, we leveraged whole-exome sequencing to create disease-specific GWAS sets using whole genome-wide expression profiles obtained from 72,651 rare disease patients in 8,422 unaffected individuals. Given that diseased patients derive from fewer genetic factors and disease specific RNA isoforms, we create our pathogenicity data sets (PDAs) to permit dissection by biological pathways and simultaneously generate GWAS statistics. The concept of learning-edge predictors and pathway harmonization is used to derive robust disease GWAS sets, guided by GWAS evidence in diseased individuals and using pathways that are conditional and pleiotropic. This presents a reliable and streamlined method to build consensus disease GWAS sets.

Predictive models based on deep learning (deep-clean) models are significantly underused in clinical diagnostics, and there is a large unmet need in this space. Here, we propose deep diagnostics on top of a second-order plasminogen-time (2dPt) signature. De-escalating two predictors that lead to threshold values of fewer than 1500 counts at clinical discharge have a sensitivity of 74.3% and specificity of 52.7%. The model is scalable and computational and can be trained using publicly available RNA-seq and FastQC data, thereby supporting broad applicability. This discovery demonstrates that accurate 2dPt prediction is feasible on a widely available set of sequencing data and is robust across multiple pan-cancer and multiple-sample cancer types. Using deep-level clustering and stratified random sampling, we assessed the uncertainty of the diagnostic model, with a focus on the importance of deep learning in predicting patterns of disease and treatment decisions in clinical practice. We demonstrate that using 2dPt prediction in serial testing to facilitate early treatment is supported by our approach. Deep-level clustering of RNA-seq data is an alternative approach for developing highly predictive, incremental diagnostic models.
sample_p_texts: Sequence-to-function models can predict gene expression from sequence data and be used to link genetic information with transcriptomics data to understand regulatory processes and their effects on complex phenotypes. The genomic language models are pre-trained with large-scale DNA sequences and can generate robust representations of these sequences by learning the genomic context. However, few studies can estimate the predictability of gene expression levels and bridge these two classes of models together to explore individualized gene expression prediction. In this manuscript, we propose UKBioBERT as a DNA language model pre-trained with genetic variants from UK BioBank. We demonstrate that UKBioBERT generates informative embeddings capable of identifying gene functions, and improving gene expression prediction in cell lines, thereby enhancing our understanding of gene expression predictability. Building upon these embeddings, we combine UKBioBERT with state-of-the-art sequence-to-function architectures, Enformer and Borzoi, to create UKBioFormer and UKBioZoi. These models exhibit better performance in predicting highly predictable gene expression levels and can be generalized across different cohorts. Furthermore, UKBioFormer effectively captures the relationship between genetic variants and expression variations, enabling in-silico mutation analyses. Collectively, our findings underscore the value of integrating genomic language models and sequence-to-function approaches for advancing functional genomics research.

Sequence-to-function analysis is a challenging task in human genetics, especially in predicting cell-type-specific multi-omic phenotypes from biological sequences such as individualized gene expression. Here, we present UNICORN, a new method with improved prediction performances than the existing methods. UNI-CORN takes the embeddings from biological sequences as well as external knowledge from pre-trained foundation models as inputs and optimizes the predictor with carefully-designed loss functions. We demonstrate that UNICORN outperforms the existing methods in both gene expression prediction and multiomic phenotype prediction at the cellular level and the cell-type level, and it can also generate uncertainty scores of the predictions. Moreover, UNICORN is able to link personalized gene expression profiles with corresponding genome information. Finally, we show that UNICORN is capable of characterizing complex biological systems for different disease states or perturbations. Overall, embeddings from foundation models can facilitate the understanding of the role of biological sequences in the prediction task, and incorporating multi-omic information can enhance prediction performances.

Deep learning sequence to function models can predict the molecular effects of genetic variants, but their predictions are limited to the cell types and assays they are trained on. Here we describe DNACipher, a deep learning model that predicts the effects of genetic variants across diverse biological contexts--including those not directly measured. DNACipher takes 196 kb of genome sequences as input and imputes variant effects across 38,582 cell type-assay combinations. DNACipher generates predictions for >7 times as many contexts as Enformer, which allows for better detection of variant effects at expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). We also introduce DNACipher Deep Variant Impact Mapping (DVIM), a method to identify variants with molecular effects at genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci. Application of DVIM to type 1 diabetes (T1D) reduced the mean fine-mapping credible set size from 24 to 1.4 variants per signal. DVIM variants had significantly higher fine-mapping posterior probabilities, and their predicted effects were supported by single-nucleus ATAC-seq and luciferase assays. DVIM also detected 6547 rare variants with molecular effects at 96% of GWAS T1D loci, and these were enriched for associations with immune traits. In summary, DNACipher DVIM prioritises common and rare variants at GWAS loci by predicting molecular effects across a broad range of contexts.

Interpretation of variants identified during genetic testing is a significant clinical challenge. In this study, we developed a high-throughput CDKN2A functional assay and characterized all possible CDKN2A missense variants. We found that 17.7% of all missense variants were functionally deleterious. We also used our functional classifications to assess the performance of in silico models that predict the effect of variants, including recently reported models based on machine learning. Notably, we found that all in silico models performed similarly when compared to our functional classifications with accuracies of 39.5-85.4%. Furthermore, while we found that functionally deleterious variants were enriched within ankyrin repeats, we did not identify any residues where all missense variants were functionally deleterious. Our functional classifications are a resource to aid the interpretation of CDKN2A variants and have important implications for the application of variant interpretation guidelines, particularly the use of in silico models for clinical variant interpretation.

Models for mutation effect prediction in coding sequences rely on sequence-, structure-, or homology-based features. Here, we introduce a novel method that combines a codon language model with a protein language model, providing a dual representation for evaluating effects of mutations on disease. By capturing contextual dependencies at both the genetic and protein level, our approach achieves a 3% increase in ROC-AUC classifying disease effects for 137,350 ClinVar missense variants across 13,791 genes, outperforming two single-sequence-based language models. Obviously the codon language model can uniquely differentiate synonymous from nonsense mutations at the genomic level. Our strategy uses information at complementary biological scales (akin to human multilingual models) to enable protein fitness landscape modeling and evolutionary studies, with potential applications in precision medicine, protein engineering, and genomics.

Many machine learning methods can be applied to predicting phenotypes from genetic data. Which of these methods work best remains an open question, however. To answer this question, we propose to compare a variety of approaches ability to predict a simulated non-linear complex trait. Specifically, we evaluate these methods on their accuracy and scalability with respect to the amount training data available, the noise present in the data, the complexity of the simulated (trait) functions, and their ability to provide insight into the simulated trait. We then compare the best approach to state-of-the-art models in real data, predicting gout in the UK Biobank. We find that transformer encoders outperform all other methods in simulations, and perform comparably to the state-of-the-art with real data, with a promise to scale to significantly larger datasets.

sample_q_texts: The availability of modern high-resolution multi-omics data has enabled researchers to study rare diseases with newly discovered mutations. Currently, these data are fragmented, making it challenging to infer how they can integrate together to predict biological consequences. Here, we introduce a methodological approach that links structural features from the biological component of the experimentally acquired data in a reference-free form with time-invariant sequence information from the genomic component. We created a publicly available computational framework, named E-IncoC, integrating the reference-free structure, order, and sequence information of a dataset into a single nucleotide resolution. Furthermore, we propose a novel set of methods designed to augment this information, including a residue-based signature of the likelihood of amino acid change and a robust signature of mutation rate (MRR). We use these approaches to analyze five single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and mutation datasets to demonstrate the power of the proposed framework and potential clinical applications. In particular, our SNP dataset identifies mutations that are unique to clinical samples, and our mutation dataset provides a list of age-dependent mutations in current selection programs. We expect the proposed framework will aid researchers in interpreting the genetic information contained in human and animal genetic data to expand clinical applications of these tools and promote their application for different research aims.

Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) provides comprehensive genomic data, but with insufficient depth and heterogeneity to completely resolve lineage and developmental differences between cell types in the same tissue. Strategies exist to overcome this limitation, including whole-exome sequencing and targeted sequencing of specific genes, both of which present unique challenges. We used genomic data from young goats for the high throughput, genotype-specific analysis of 575 WT calves between two age groups and 14 other genetic strains. We measured both nucleic acid and RNA-seq to compare lineage effects and discovered that targeting specific genes at low coverage can reveal lineage differences; however, the lack of genomic data from unrelated tissues means that studies using WGS should make greater use of RNA-seq to isolate and examine any possible lineage effects. The experiment generated 510K+ sequence reads for all samples. Fifty-three percent of the samples were enriched for 50,000-6,000 reads on the level of total reads, which are highly fragmented by DNA-cutting enzymes, including red-orange, and with a median read length of 38-850 base pairs. We designed a pipeline, read4train, that was optimized to reassemble sequence data into accessible form, producing annotated reads that were: 1) size-adjusted to be sequence-enriched in multiple respects; 2) a) adapted to the sequence data types, b) coupled into a library of sequenced-files for individual studies; 3) mapped onto sequence families; 4) reassembled from fragment assemblies into contiguous genome reads; 5) arranged by mapping sites in order of expression; and 6) paired against the goat genome to study variability in what was present. We were able to identify and validate a single cell that had not previously been named as developmentally-zoned during case-scratches, based on the different methylation of an alphaC-synuclein-interfering DNA element. We assembled enough reads to understand the high proportion of reads in each sequence category, a protocol-informed prediction of each gene that could have multiple transcription events during an open reading frame, which increased computational complexity with which to resequence data. The large read number and the use of multiple short sequences resulted in high prediction complexity for analysis, and did not produce stable reassemblies. Some genes within multiple gene families presented distinct, or limited, haplotypes. We conclude that WGS can resolve lineage differences and has the potential to inform relevant developmental research, but that it does

The ability to adapt mutations in an individual's genetic code over time remains a challenge in contemporary analyses of evolution, with techniques designed for genomic snapshots often insufficient to address modern issues. For complex systems like human biology, where many mutations are rare, accumulating over the lifespan poses a challenge for mathematical modelling and phylogenetic inference. Our study presents a non-parametric, scalable and high-performing approach that extends the current tool suite for studying rare mutations in the IntRON-B locus, a critical gene in Prader-Willi Syndrome. Utilizing shared genetic homology and inheritance analysis, we demonstrate that this model may be extended to address the changing environments of complex genomes, and potentially provide an enabling environment for the analysis of intricate natural phenomena. By applying this model, we aimed to extract the "meta-normality" of frequency-adjusted variance-covariance structure, a powerful set of scaling measures for "omics" datasets. We first used this expanded analysis to identify one newly discovered population genetic association. Applying phylogenetic theory, we confirm this association can be explained by mutation rates from before sequencing time periods, and establish that various axes of divergence have a common underlying origin. Our models reveal that while rare mutations are more important in males and females than in entire populations, genome-wide data reveal genetic discordance at the order level, emphasizing the importance of sex-specific patterns. Furthermore, the expansion of the model improves power to detect patterns that are severely affected by the mutation rate at which the target gene is under-represented, like those related to telomere, an example of which is how the distribution of deviations from SRY gene origin in humans and fish evolved. Importantly, this model can be extended and applied to diverse species.

The human genome encodes 30 structural variants (SVs), i.e. homoeologs, that differ from 113 divergent sequences encompassing the human genome. There is mounting evidence that SVs are not SNPs and have thus the potential to impact common function. Here, we elucidate two key aspects of SV pathogenesis using an unbiased and global observational strategy. Analysis of pre- and post-splicing regions of SVs in depth reveals tissue-specific splicing biases across regions, providing evidence for the co-evolution of RNA-binding proteins with splicing in SVs. This suggests that specific SVs orchestrate essential biological processes under specific transcriptomic conditions, with the potential for disease. Specifically, we report that TSS differences, rather than genetic variation, predict body weight changes, with some even age-related in human tissues. Our analyses suggest novel molecular couplings between transcripts and chromatin that drive developmental processes and identify the genotype-environment coupling for obesity. Our insights augment genome-wide understanding of SV function in complex developmental processes.

Lateral Ventricular (LV) segmentation is a fundamental process of cortical structure development. Cohesion and proliferation have been shown to govern segmentation, but the mechanism behind this function remains unknown. Ligation-based alignment is widely used in molecular biology to connect peptide ligands with DNA sequences, which could be used to identify key mechanisms that govern segmentation. In this work, we present a method to link a sequence-guided alignment (SGA) ensemble of cis-interspersed elements (CIEs) to the sequence-specific DNA sequence with the help of a sequence-similarity (SS) score-based criterion. We first identified 77,905 complete LSU-SS datasets containing full-length whole-genome loci, and then generated an SGA ensemble of 7,517 contiguous stretches of single-nucleotide variation (SNVs) in 8,324 full-length murine intronic genes (ILGs) via partial linkage and selected matches based on SCCs (supercalling continuous sequences), identified by GENOTCH (Genotyping for identification, Characterization, Transcriptional Profile and search for annotation in long and small genomes). Mutations were predicted using three alignment strategies: (1) contextual SCCs, (2) ON-BY-OFFs (one forward, one reverse), and (3) not hot-spots (SNVs bound to seven genes with more than 10 mutations in the engine). Consensus events obtained by the three strategies were used for CCG feature spaces, encoding 143,677 unique regions of either one or more segments, segmented into six conserved LSP regions (LS-I~6). Selection was performed on these regions of interest (LOIs), which were anchored into gene structures by the definition of LC-type CMS (Loop-Cancelated Segmentation Modularity) as the criterion. The criteria-based annotation revealed that each segment enriched for the addition and deletion of a DNA base. Moreover, the LOIs hosted all known mutations, but in contrast, the majority of mutations had only a splice junction within the remaining sequence (p<0.05). Key segments were high-scoring according to the criteria, and most of the mutations were primarily insertion (N41 in 12/14 genes, 1/117 sites; N42 in 15 genes, 7/61 sites; N46 in 15 genes, 12/61 sites; N47 in 12 genes, 1

Genetic variation, which influences critical processes like chromatin dynamics and gene expression, has been recognized as a critical component of complex developmental trajectories. We assessed the contribution of nucleotide variant, constructed on a 2nt resolution shotgun sequencing, to regions encoding a set of 31 involved residues, binding to seven-amino-acid transmembrane peptide receptors. The receptors under consideration span biological and therapeutic relevance, including glycogen synthase (GnS), lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh), AMP-activated proteases, hERG, sodium-sodium channel, farnesyl diphosphate-binding phosphodiesterase 6 (Fpn6), and human leptin (Hln). Using quantitative mass spectrometry, we performed site-directed mutagenesis and assessed residue-level variant-induced post-translational modifications. We found that 120nt DNA target sites conferred significant post-translational changes, enhancing affinity for the receptors with which they paired. A pairwise correlation analysis revealed that the proteins with the greatest DNA-binding affinity typically showed the strongest post-translationally modified sites. We identified 612 potential amino acids critical for site-specific post-translational modification events. The majority of these sites are positioned within short but biologically conserved amino acids predicted to be excluded from post-translational modification. Using mutation scanning of a single amino acid, we inferred that this asymmetry in these hydrophobic sites was likely due to non-random post-translational adjustments in an otherwise unbiased second proofreading mechanism. Thus, we found that post-translational modifications of residues critical for site-specific protein-ligand interactions contribute to strength of adhesion and tissue specificity in ligand-mediated sensory transduction.

A genetic variant (rs622424) in the novel splice donor sequence of the alpha-globin gene is associated with accelerated expression of alpha-globin mRNA. Furthermore, its replication precedes alpha-globin expression and localization, and involvement in the DNA replication cycle. However, its evolutionary and disease association with alpha-globin disease is not clear. Here, we analyze the structural features of the alpha-globin gene to identify the specific binding elements and the regulatory elements upstream of rs622424. We show that certain mutations in the alpha-globin structural repeat motif lead to temporal inactivation of rs622424 but also accelerated encoding. Furthermore, these mutations result in accelerated alpha-globin mRNA levels and of local expression and localization of rs622424. Finally, functional analysis and reverse genetics studies indicate that the rs622424 mutation strongly correlates with accelerated alpha-globin expression and cellular expression of alpha-globin and arginine 488. We further study how rs622424 mutations regulate alpha-globin function. We demonstrate that the rs622424 mutation strongly accelerates alpha-globin mRNA levels and alpha-globin expression and localization. Furthermore, mutations in rs622424 promote alpha-globin cell localization and changes in alpha-globin transcriptional activity. Taken together, our data reveal that the alpha-globin structural repeat motif plays a critical role in the regulation of alpha-globin expression.

The human genome encodes approximately 21,000 genes (inter alia, exons, non-exons and alternative transcripts) that code for proteins. Human genomes are uniquely characterized by an extraordinary level of repeat polymorphism, indicating that the genetic information encoded by the genome is highly adaptive. One such class of repeat polymorphism, telomeric DNA (TDP), encodes DNA binding proteins that interact with telomeric protein complexes, which regulate genetic activities of the genome including transcription, recombination, and replication. TDPs are one of the most abundant gene families in mammals and hence form a crucial component of a host genome. This functional units can constitute about 2% of the human genome and most of these repeats are pseudogenes.

We have been attempting to elucidate the involvement of TDP repeats in human diseases. Our work shows that each individual clone (telomere) can exist either as a wildtype type (WT) or a mutant variant (mutant). Our computational studies with a computational framework have characterized a set of predictions related to these two types of variants for possible pathogenic effects.

BackgroundDefects in tandem repeats (TRs) play critical roles in a range of diseases, particularly in aging populations. The progression of TRs involves both turnover and end-replication, which may differ between tissue types and age groups. However, the mechanisms underlying the overlap between the turnover and end-replication of TRs in different biological contexts remain poorly understood.

Aim We analyzed longitudinally acquired phase-shifted sequencing data of RNA-Seq datasets of 50 individuals with sporadic and syndromic TR tumors. We identified which regions of the mRNA transcripts amplified at different rates and their respective full-length transcript isoforms.

Results To characterize the nature of TRs, we aligned the associated time-series transcriptomes to align with the full-length RNA-seq reads, using a phylogenetic model-based alignment approach. Significant differences in the transcriptomic data signal that individual RNA isoforms expand at different rates. At the C-terminus, TRs show most variation, with a ratio between expansion rates of ~27:1 in TR13C and 10:1 in TR13C2. Similar differences in TR15C are also observed, with a ratio of ~100:1 in TR15C and ~30:1 in TR15C2. Compared to the transcripts for the 10 genes that were duplicated, these TRs have differences in isoform abundance in the C-terminus. These differences were not evident in the 54 genes that were not duplicated. These data can be used as a basis for identifying patients with affected TR isoforms.

DiscussionCompared to the underlying protein sequences, TR length is linked to length of mRNA isoforms of the gene. To uncover such relations, we used alignment-based methods to identify the regions that show the greatest biological variance in expression. However, differences between isoforms do not explain the variance in expression. We conclude that TRs represent aging processes, which might be linked to genes with a constitutive regulatory network.

SignificanceStatement Trends in differential mRNAs across tissues show that some of these poly-dipeptides (EDTs) are characteristic of aging. These links explain how the genetic gains in different tissues and days of life are reflected in each individual body clock of the biological and institutional body clocks and related tissues.

Human genomes are consistently smaller than the corresponding genomes in the nonhuman 45S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) transcriptome. However, sophisticated computational modelling challenges this hypothesis by demonstrating that many of the genomic base-pair substitutions found in the rRNAs can be due to the incorporation of extra bases in the nucleosomes.

Here, we demonstrate that this rule applies for both human and Neanderthal genomes using large, paired databases from the Human Reference Genome (HRG; 200Mb) dataset and Neander Valley (NV). We discovered that the nucleosomes in the unprocessed genomic regions, including intergenic regions, are particularly well-characterised as they cannot be extracted efficiently from reads in the long read read datasets.

The nucleosome base-pair statistics derived from 2622 VCFs and alignment with micro-scopic detail were designed to show that most of the nucleosomes inserted into the intergenic regions are derived from long-range N-nitrosylation in the nucleosome, not the unmodified basepairs.

Although we uncovered a database size constraint for rRNAs, this is consistent with the known constraints in other biological data, such as genome assemblies and assembled genomes, which dictate the size of the base-pair detection set for certain bases at a genome-wide scale. We validated the nucleosome determination and multiple base reading frames with an independent genomics pipeline and similar conclusions for animal genomes.

The non-nucleosomal annotations are important base pairs, or 18bp indel-based insertions and deletions that can generate many outcomes including somatic tumours.
sample_p_texts: Tandem repeats are a class of genetic variation characterized by repetitions of DNA motifs of diverse sequences and lengths. Pentameric motifs, in particular, do not align with the protein-coding reading frames, often confining them to the less extensively studied non-coding portion of the genome. Intronic pentanucleotide tandem repeats are associated with 11 neurological disorders. Their pathogenic genotypes are primarily characterized by large length expansion and, unlike most repeat expansion disorders, have required a deviation from the reference motif. The population-level variability of pentameric repeats remains poorly understood due to technical limitations of short-read sequencing technologies. To address this knowledge gap, we genotyped 28,446 pentanucleotide repeat loci in 1,027 long-read PacBio HiFi samples from self-identified Black and African American participants in the All of Us Research Program. We developed new algorithms for tandem repeat decomposition, characterization, and visualization to facilitate this analysis. Our findings reveal extensive genome-wide heterogeneity in repeat length and sequence composition. Alleles with DNA sequences containing segments of distinct motifs were observed in 15% of loci. Additionally, 8% of loci exhibited multimodal repeat length distributions, in which distinct sequence compositions were often associated with distinct length ranges. Repeat loci were highly enriched in proximity to transposable elements, including 68% mapping to Alu elements, a retrotransposon specific to primates. Comparative analysis of the reference sequences from 30 species, including 27 primates, suggests that most pentanucleotide repeats fully emerged in a common ancestor of humans and other ape species, or even within more closely related hominin lineages. As an example, we describe a highly polymorphic and recently evolved repeat locus in the ABCA1 gene, a major regulator of cellular cholesterol and phospholipid homeostasis. This study provides novel and comprehensive insights into the evolutionary formation of pentamer tandem repeat loci and their extensive variability across human genomes.

Single-stranded RNA molecules can form intramolecular bonds between nucleotides to create secondary structures. These structures can have phenotypic effects, meaning mutations that alter secondary structure may be subject to natural selection. Here we examined the population genetics of these mutations within Arabidopsis thaliana genes. We began by identifying derived SNPs with the potential to alter secondary structures within coding regions, using a combination of computational prediction and empirical data analysis. We identified 8,469 such polymorphisms, representing a small portion ([~]0.024%) of sites within transcribed genes. We examined nucleotide diversity and allele frequencies of these "pair-changing mutations" (pcM) in 1,001 A. thaliana genomes. The pcM SNPs at synonymous sites had an 13.4% reduction in nucleotide diversity relative to non-pcM SNPs at synonymous sites and were found at lower allele frequencies. We used demographic modeling to estimate selection coefficients, finding selection against pcMs in 5 and 3 untranslated regions. Previous work has shown that some pcMs affect gene expression in a temperature-dependent matter. We explored associations on a genome-wide scale, finding pcMs exist at higher population frequencies in colder environments, as do non-PCM alleles. Derived pcM mutations have a small but significant relationship to transcript abundance, however; alleles containing pcMs had an average reduction in expression of 137.4 normalized counts compared to genes with conserved ancestral secondary structure (mean expression = 3215.7 normalized counts). Overall, we document selection against derived pcMs in UTRs but with limited evidence for selection against derived pcMs at synonymous sites.

The ribosome is one of the core macromolecules in the cell. The ribosomal RNAs (rRNA), which are essential components of the ribosome, are coded by the multi-copy ribosomal DNA (rDNA). Despite its highly conserved function, the rDNA displays substantial variation within all species analysed to date. This variation comprises both inter-individual differences in total copy number (CN) as well as inter- and intragenomic sequence variation in the form of single nucleotide variants (SNV) and insertions/deletions (INDELs) across rDNA copies. Whether germline variation of rDNA sequence associates with phenotypic traits in humans is, to date, unknown. Here, using the UK Biobank whole genome sequencing data, we first derive a high confidence list of rDNA-associated SNVs and INDELs that we validate in multiple ways. Using this list, we show that specific rDNA variants associate with several human traits. In particular, traits associated with body size appear enriched in variants within the Expansion Segment 15L region in the 28S rRNA. The strength of these associations does not diminish when accounting for the total rDNA CN of each individual. Our work represents the first large-scale association analysis of human traits with germline sequence variation in the rDNA, a source of human complex trait-relevant genetic variation that has thus far been largely ignored.

Somatic variants accumulate in non-malignant tissues with age1,2. Functional variants leading to clonal advantage of hepatocytes accumulate in the liver from patients with acquired chronic liver disease (CLD)3-5. Whether these somatic variants are common to CLD from differing aetiologies is unknown. We analysed somatic variants in the liver from patients with genetic CLD from alpha-1 anti-trypsin (A1AT) deficiency or haemochromatosis. We show that somatic variants in SERPINA1, the gene encoding A1AT, are strongly selected for in A1AT deficiency, with evidence of convergent evolution. Acquired variants cluster at the 3 end of SERPINA1 leading to C-terminal missense or truncation variants of A1AT. In vitro, C-terminal truncation variants abrogate disease-associated A1AT polymerisation and retention in the endoplasmic reticulum, supporting the C-terminal domain swap mechanism. Therefore, somatic escape variants from a deleterious germline variant are selected for in A1AT deficiency, suggesting adaptive functional somatic variants are disease-specific in CLD and point to disease-associated mechanisms.

Supergenes are linked clusters of DNA that are transmitted together due to rare or absent recombination. They undergo co-adaptation, allowing evolution to work on several genes to refine complex phenotypes, giving supergenes a competitive edge. Yet, due to their lack of recombination, supergenes are susceptible to deterioration as they cannot efficiently purge deleterious DNA. Few examples outside of sex chromosomes have been available for study. Here, we present the first assembly of the t haplotype, a 33.4 Mb supergene in house mice that  selfishly transmits itself at non-Mendelian frequencies. We characterize the four large non-overlapping inversions that make up the t haplotype. We compare in a t/t individual two different t variants with different recessive lethal phenotypes (age at death). Despite that difference, they differ much less from each other than the rest of the chromosome. However, the differences that they have were much more likely to be deleterious than the differences between the two variants of the rest of the chromosome. We interpret this marked difference as evidence of the accumulation of deleterious variants, a hallmark of deterioration. The t region of chromosome 17 is more distant to the reference than the rest of the chromosome, and has a higher fraction of impactful differences here as well. Thus, we conclude that the t appears as a quickly spreading and deteriorating selfish supergene, a rare example of Mullers ratchet outside of sex chromosomes. Furthermore, we aim for our assembly to provide a resource for comparative work on the t haplotype, such as its evolutionary history.

The HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) is the only worldwide authority that assigns standardised nomenclature to human genes (1). All studies related to the human genome and genes worldwide should adhere to HGNC-approved gene names and symbols, emphasizing the importance of precise classification and naming. Recent studies have revealed the functional and clinical relevance of RNU2-2P, which is linked to neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer (2-4), underscoring the need to reassess the classification of pseudogenes and functional non-coding RNA genes. In this study, we explore the conservation and expression of genes from 15 small ncRNA families, including U1, U2, U4, U5, U6, U4ATAC, U6ATAC, U11, U12, Vault tRNA (VTRNA), Y RNA, tRNA, 7SL, U7, and 7SK, to identify non-coding RNA-derived pseudogenes that are under strong negative selection in the human genome. Our findings highlight three highly conserved and expressed pseudogenes--RNU2-2P, RNU1-27P, and RNU1-28P--that are likely misclassified, as existing evidence suggests they may play a role in disease research. This warrants a reevaluation of their status as pseudogenes. Additionally, we identified RNU5F-1, a functional copy of RNU5, which is lowly conserved and expressed, yet its classification as a functional gene raises questions about its potential role. Furthermore, other pseudogenes and functional ncRNAs that could also be misclassified were identified, suggesting the necessity for further experimental and clinical examination.

Most mammalian genes undergo alternative splicing. The splicing of some exons has been acquired or lost in specific mammalian lineages, but differences in splicing within the human population are poorly characterized. Using GTEx tissue transcriptomes from 838 individuals, we identified 56,415 exons which are included in mRNAs in some individuals but entirely excluded from others, which we term "naturally variable exons" (NVEs). NVEs impact three quarters of protein-coding genes, occur at all population frequencies, and are often absent from reference annotations. NVEs are more abundant in genes depleted of genetic loss-of-function mutations and aid in the interpretation of causal genetic variants. Genetic variants modulate the splicing of many NVEs, and 5UTR and coding-region NVEs are often associated with increased and decreased gene expression, respectively. Together, our findings characterize abundant splicing variation in the human population, with implications for a range of human genetic analyses.

One of the strongest signatures of aging is an accumulation of mutant mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy. Here we investigate the mechanism underlying this phenomenon by calling mtDNA sequence, abundance, and heteroplasmic variation in human blood using whole genome sequences from [~]750,000 individuals. Our analyses reveal a simple, two-step mechanism: first, individual cells randomly accumulate low levels of "cryptic" mtDNA mutations; then, when a cell clone proliferates, the cryptic mtDNA variants are carried as passenger mutations and become detectable in whole blood. Four lines of evidence support this model: (1) the mutational spectrum of age-accumulating mtDNA variants is consistent with a well-established model of mtDNA replication errors, (2) these mutations are found primarily at low levels of heteroplasmy and do not show evidence of positive selection, (3) high mtDNA mutation burden tends to co-occur in samples harboring somatic driver mutations for clonal hematopoiesis (CH), and (4) nuclear GWAS reveals that germline variants predisposing to CH (such as those near TERT, TCL1A, and SMC4) also increase mtDNA mutation burden. We propose that the high copy number and high mutation rate of mtDNA make it a particularly sensitive blood-based marker of CH. Importantly, our work helps to mechanistically unify three prominent signatures of aging: common germline variants in TERT, clonal hematopoiesis, and observed mtDNA mutation accrual.

The NPIP (nuclear pore interacting protein) gene family has expanded to high copy number in humans and African apes where it has been subject to an excess of amino acid replacement consistent with positive selection (1). Due to the limitations of short-read sequencing, NPIP human genetic diversity has been poorly understood. Using highly accurate assemblies generated from long-read sequencing as part of the human pangenome, we completely characterize 169 human haplotypes (4,665 NPIP paralogs and alleles). Of the 28 NPIP paralogs, just three (NPIPB2, B11, and B14) are fixed at a single copy, and only a single locus, B2, shows no structural variation. Four NPIP paralogs map to large segmental duplication blocks that mediate polymorphic inversions (355 kbp-1.6 Mbp) corresponding to microdeletions associated with developmental delay and autism. Haplotype-based tests of positive selection and selective sweeps identify two paralogs, B9 and B15, within the top percentile for both tests. Using full-length cDNA data from 101 tissue/cell types, we construct paralog-specific gene models and show that 56% (31/55 most abundant isoforms) have not been previously described in RefSeq. We define six distinct translation start sites and other protein structural features that distinguish paralogs, including a variable number tandem repeat that encodes a beta helix of variable size that emerged [~]3.1 million years ago in human evolution. Among the 28 NPIP paralogs, we identify distinct tissue and developmental patterns of expression with only a few maintaining the ancestral testis-enriched expression. A subset of paralogs (NPIPA1, A5, A6-9, B3-5, and B12/B13) show increased brain expression. Our results suggest ongoing positive selection in the human population and rapid diversification of NPIP gene models.

While most protein-coding regions in our genome are highly conserved, phenotypic variation largely arises from differences in gene transcription, splicing, and translation. Intra-gene splicing variations are a known source of inter-individual differences. However, inter-gene splicing events, which generate fusion transcripts--RNA molecules combining exons from multiple distinct genes--are less explored. Fusion transcripts are well-studied in cancer, but their expression and inter-individual variability in normal human tissues has not been thoroughly investigated. We conducted a genome-wide fusion transcript analysis in postmortem human brain tissues from 276 individuals, identifying 717 distinct fusion transcripts. Many had protein coding potential, further supported in some cases by ribosome profiling data. Fusion transcripts that were present in only part of the human population were predominantly located within segmental duplication (SD) "hotspots"; highly copy number-variable genomic regions linked to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases. None of these variable fusion transcripts were present in chimpanzee or rhesus macaque, suggesting they are human-specific. We confirmed that SD-derived fusion transcripts arise from structural genomic rearrangements in the human population, previously associated with neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease risk. Inter-individual variation in fusion transcript expression represents an overlooked source of genetic diversity, with potential to contribute to differences in disease susceptibility.

The world is a massively connected, network-like machine. We highlight common observations regarding how this network evolves in key processes such as cell fusion, docking, membrane fission, and the adhesion of cells. We show that cancer cells exploit the network in the construction of their networks by removing hub features in the network. Hub features are produced by engulfing specific pores into transmembrane domains. This sets the network up for specific interactions, e.g. with certain bacteria; they are therefore hallmarks of cancer. This implies that removing hub features from the network could give a boost to cancer treatment.

HighlightsKey Findings-Selected Hub Features Are Bypassed by Hydra Vacuole Fusion-Hub Features Are Naive Bypassed by Tissue Feeder Growth-A Design Principle For Setting Up The Network in Cancer-Cell Fusion Expands Possible Hub Features as the Network Grows-To Truly Increase Cure, Reduce Hub Features

Molecular mechanisms underlying human illness and ageing involve signalling pathways integrated in intricate genomic and transcriptomic networks. Here we sought to identify and understand such networks at the earliest stages of human ageing, aiming to gain insight into potential therapeutic avenues for disease interventions. We utilized Network Biomonitoring, developing a user-friendly computational tool for analysing gene expression networks over 100 years of human healthcare data. We identified disease stages and established the presence of adaptive networks by associating them with gene-wise terminal nodes. We systematically characterised temporal patterns in well-performing networks through variation of global architecture and the use of dynamic programming in expressing relations between nodes. Through this method, we highlight intrinsic dynamic properties of networks, uncovering adaptive mutations that have evolved over long lifespans. Our network analysis revealed that rare and durable interactions between previously linked genes led to later and more efficient network architecture, coupled with a population of tumour-associated genes and epistatic networks. This is in contrast to the patterns observed in aging relative to the proteome and cellular activity of human ageing tissues, where it suggests an earlier origin and contribution to ageing.

The main purpose of proteomics data analysis is the visualization and comprehensive discovery of biological functions. Two major challenges are that biological functions may be unfamiliar or invasive. The latter is challenging to address as currently, highly accurate methods only can compute the predicted functional linkages between protein modules under static conditions. While some classifiers can also identify unexpected functional relationships, their general applicability to variable environments is limited due to the difficulty of accurately mapping from functional knowledge to observed outcomes. We developed an adaptive method to integrate unsupervised and supervised classification. Initially, we examined a large dataset of protein-protein interactions, which led to the annotation of a molecular network consisting of hundreds of a priori linkages. Here, we have applied the strategy to an online microfluidic sensor. This application revealed the potential to identify the state of flux within a large pandemic of Covid-19. We thus designed an algorithm for proteomic-based systemic response of the whole human body to covid-19 outbreak, inferring a relationship between the global proportions of different small nuclear ribonucleic acid-based factors and the high infection risk. This algorithm allowed us to answer a whole-body statistical simulation model of Covid-19 effects based on network data rather than purely on the observed data. This allowed us to forecast to what extent the virus could cause lung infections in the far future by quantifying long-term infection. This opened the door to a potential treatment or preventive approach by early intervention, which could counteract the effect of the viral load in the initial phase of the pandemic.

Generation and analysis of large datasets, such as the 31B encephalitis dataset, presents challenges for neural network models. The advancement of computational biology, however, provides avenues for generating comprehensive, statistically robust models. In this work, we introduce CellShot as a 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the 31B dataset. We compare CellShot with various CNN architectures and suggests how it improves predictions over conventional methods. We validate CellShot on a real-world 2.6B datasets generated by the United Kingdom Bioinformatics Institute and the Racket Database for Oscillating River Flow, respectively, which contain a total of over 50,000 individuals. CellShot outperforms leading state-of-the-art CNNs such as EssigNet, InhibitorNet, and EyeNet-3.0. All three were applied to diverse real-world datasets. CellShot trained on the 2.6B Racket dataset obtained superior prediction performance compared to the best performer. It also outperforms some state-of-the-art state-of-the-art CNNs in terms of relative accuracy (RA) and their mean correlations (Mcr). The median measure of absolute error (MAE) was 0.7974 for CellShot and 0.6693 for CellShot-Mclr. CellShot had a faster learning rate at a training time of 40s, with an average loss of -2.23E-03 with a small adjustment to the loss threshold to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.

Gene-based regulatory networks (GBRNs) represent intricate interactions between regulatory elements and genes. However, the detection of regulatory interactions within the GBGRN remains challenging, particularly in its environmental conditions. In this work, we create and evaluate a platform that combines a deep representation network with a deep convolutional neural network (DRNet-DeepCNN), capable of discovering and classifying gene-regulatory features within a GBGRN based on gene expression data. The effectiveness of the proposed novel platform in detecting regulatory interactions and differentiating mRNA expression samples is demonstrated with benchmark data. To evaluate the performance of the proposed DRNet-DeepCNN, we conduct extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets and image-induced datasets. We benchmark the proposed platform on numerous public benchmarks datasets including colon cancer, brain tumor, and Parkinson's disease datasets. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed platform exhibits superior performance in identifying regulatory features associated with breast and prostate cancer cell lines, cell lines isolated from human colon tissue, and the transcriptomes from human primary brain tumor and prostate cancer tissues. It effectively identifies key regulatory interactions with several subtypes of prostate cancer. The state-of-the-art results using a state-of-the-art binary network are reported.

We propose a sequential programming flowgraph (S-RPG) that can construct and test emergent biological structures, such as proteins and DNA. Specifically, we need to model the order of events in a living cell, such as identifying a substrate in a cell by using a substrate orientation detector (SO detector). The use of SO detectors in biologically significant systems requires high levels of unsupervised learning and interpretation. To tackle this challenge, our method maps critical observable states to amino acids that define the SO detector, introduces a graph generation strategy, and performs modular refinement to model the graph and subsequently fine-tune the model. We applied the novel neural network framework to create a small amount of molecular interaction data on amino acids of 11 proteins and two DNA molecules. Our model identified sufficient amino acids for protein coding, but did not generate full SO detectors. Instead, it allows quantitative exploration of the interaction probabilities between ligands and acceptors and consequently the biological relevance of a protein-protein interaction network.

Synthetic Biology is a way of engineering living cells and tissues, which differs from conventional cell-based engineering in that only its functions are designed and may not always be observed. While there is a growing number of comprehensive and widely-used computational methods for describing biological interactions, they often lack capacity to connect important underlying biological processes within the integrated organism. Here, we aim to fill this gap by constructing a single and general tool that includes the capacity for continuous, globally interactive simulations of whole systems, and which is based on an object-oriented modeling paradigm. We called this the Overarching Simulation Engine, or OSE, and it is designed to represent complex dynamics between multiple species in regulated biological systems, and to address all biological effects on cell functioning, coordination and growth. We show that OSE has been automatically trained to obtain generalizable and species-specific knowledge by virtue of the ubiquitous human relevance of the data used to train it, the profound human biases of the systems used to develop it, and the significant human value for biological systems that it implements. Finally, we construct a suite of widely applicable and useful new computational tools that are specifically designed to address key aspects of the OSE. We call these components of the OSE building blocks that can be combined to form models relevant to a variety of social, biological and biomedical problems. These include: a new generation of filtering and classification methods, a new generation of prioritization and comparison tools, a new generation of structural and network-based tools, and a new generation of routine, easy-to-use modules for these tools.

Genome-scale association network methods such as fAnalysis outperform traditional association methods because they include tissue- or cell-specific restrictions. However, resources to analyze such complex networks are rare. Here, we characterize a method that uses Differential Genome Architecture to generate association networks from omic data. This method leverages the marginal output of fAnalysis (details on the techniques in previous works, all based on the FELSID algorithm), while providing alternative methods for further filtering of annotated genes that do not overlap with biological pathways. The resulting networks do not need tissuespecific alignments to be able to explain most of the variance of genomic expression data. Furthermore, the method was able to integrate an ancillary deconvolution approach to account for expression noise. In summary, the approach provides a newly interpretable multivariate summary of genomic data that allows the discovery of hidden relations while filtering out noise that is potentially derived from physiological states. Further investigations revealed a link between chronic health conditions and metabolic defects.

The study of quantitative genetic models provides insights into the relationships between environmental factors and biological traits in both human and animals. These models can be constructed using the mathematical and computational toolkits. We introduce a system of tasks to train the existing models for the quantification of genes and pathways in physiological systems and architecture. Our approach is applied to a system model of myocardial injury in metabolic disease. It incorporates three tasks that deal with the quantification of structural and functional genes, pathways, and networks. These tasks are hierarchically interconnected in order to identify the most impactful ones for dissection. Our analyses reveal that common regulatory factors identified in different experiments and associated with other pathological processes can regulate the gene expression and function of the myocardium. Finally, we show how the constructed models can be applied to the two published quantitative genetic models. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and success of this method and provide a demonstration of its potential use in the quantitation of genetic and pathway interactions in biological systems.

Biological networks represent communities of interacting members or components and are essential in identifying and examining systems underlying biological processes. In addition to the standard input data of cells/organisms and other components available in the cell biology literature, they may also require external data such as time-series data, experimental measurements, and independent samples for complex dynamic data. We introduce a deep learning method called DiSeq20 to quantify the structural properties of networks represented as graphs. We show that DiSeq20 not only can localize regions with higher dimensional structural differences in networks but also exploits additional information, such as metabolite structure, heterocycles, isotopes, and different species with robust methods. We found that the structure of the network with only positive metabolites is more challenging for Naive Bayes detectors. A deeper dataset induced by augmentations and the enhanced adaptation strategy, DIAVID, has revealed the underlying heterogeneity in the structure of many unseen data sets. This robust transfer and adaptation strategy is theoretically based on graph priors in the reaction field. We demonstrate the robust abilities of DiSeq20 on three different datasets across two-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces: the impact of interactions between astrocytes on the cytoskeleton of blood vessel cells in de novo graphs. Furthermore, we show that the structure of the networks is better predicted by using the information extraction graph, which contains molecular type fragments. Finally, we showed that there exist a series of graphs that reveal the information of the previous training set. In addition, DiSeq20 offers several local and global supervisory strategies to orient their own supervision to inform more relevant information while leveraging the multimodal enhancement of the data.
sample_p_texts: Biochemical networks are models of biological functions and processes in biomedicine. Hierarchical decomposition simplifies complex biochemical networks by partitioning them into smaller blocks (modules), facilitating computationally intensive analyses and providing deeper insights into cellular processes and regulatory mechanisms. We introduce a novel algorithm for the hierarchical decomposition of large-scale biochemical systems. By using causality and information flow as organizing principles, our approach combines strongly connected components with r-causality to identify and structure manageable network blocks. Benchmarking against a comprehensive database of biochemical reaction networks demonstrates the computational efficiency and scalability of our algorithm. To ensure broad applicability, we integrate our algorithm into tools that support standardized Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) formats, facilitating its use in biochemical modeling workflows.

Gene interaction networks specify how genes interact to produce an organisms phenotype. These networks are often incomplete due to absent or unobserved information. Predicting these missing links is critical for many applications, including genome-wide association studies and phenotype prediction. Efforts have previously applied graph neural networks (GNNs) to this missing-link prediction problem, but these techniques too have limitations when the sparsity of the networks is very high. Here, we apply a novel feature engineering technique that uses local graph motif incidence to enhance the feature set for variational graph autoencoders (VGAE). We compare the performance of our technique against state-of-the-art approaches, and then progressively hide more and more of the original graph edges. Our results show that VGAEs with our local-area motif prevalence (LAMP) features outperform state-of-the-art node embeddings for a wide range of missing edges on both a benchmark and a biological dataset. We also observe that this combined VGAE and LAMP technique has the potential to facilitate the search for novel genetic interactions in an experimental adaptive sampling context with far fewer samples. Improvements to gene interaction imputation can lower the barrier to new pharmaceutical and epidemiological discoveries by revealing hidden gene interactions that steer the development of potential drug targets.

MotivationIdentifying meaningful patterns in complex biological data necessitates correlation coefficients capable of capturing diverse relationship types beyond simple linearity. Furthermore, efficient computational tools are crucial for handling the ever-increasing scale of biological datasets.

ResultsWe introduce CCC-GPU, a high-performance, GPU-accelerated implementation of the Clustermatch Correlation Coefficient (CCC). CCC-GPU computes correlation coefficients for mixed data types, effectively detects non-linear relationships, and offers significant speed improvements over its predecessor.

Availability and ImplementationCCC-GPU is openly available on GitHub (https://github.com/pivlab/ccc-gpu) and distributed under the BSD-2-Clause Plus Patent License.

Essential proteins are group of proteins that are indispensable to survival and development of cells. Prediction and analysis of essential genes/proteins are crucial for uncovering the mechanisms of cells. Using bioinformatics and high-throughput technologies, forecasting essential genes/proteins by protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks have become more efficient than traditional approaches which use expensive and time-consuming experimental methods. Previous studies have found that the essentiality of genes closely relates to their properties in PPI network. In this work, we propose a supervised deep model for predicting human essential genes using neighboring details of genes/proteins in the PPI network. Our approach implements a weight-biased random walk on PPI network to get the node network context. Then, some different measures are used to get some feature vectors for each node (gene/protein) that preserve the network structure as well as the genes properties in the PPI network. These feature vectors are then fed to a Relational AutoEncoder to embed the genes features into latent space. At last, these embedded features are put into a trained classifier to predict the human essential genes. The prediction results on two human PPI networks show that our model achieves better performance than those that only refer to genes centrality properties in the network.

Molecular interaction networks are a vital tool for studying biological systems. While many tools exist that visualize a protein or a pathway within a network, no tool provides the ability for a researcher to consider a proteins position in a network in the context of a specific biological process or pathway. We developed ProteinWeaver, a web-based tool designed to visualize and analyze non-human protein interaction networks by integrating known biological functions. ProteinWeaver provides users with an intuitive interface to situate a user-specified protein in a user-provided biological context (as a Gene Ontology term) in five model organisms. Protein-Weaver also reports the presence of physical and regulatory network motifs within the queried subnetwork and statistics about the proteins distance to the biological process or pathway within the network. These insights can help researchers generate testable hypotheses about the proteins potential role in the process or pathway under study. Two cell biology case studies demonstrate ProteinWeavers potential to generate hypotheses from the queried subnetworks. ProteinWeaver is available at https://proteinweaver.reedcompbio.org/.

Conducting disentanglement learning on single-cell omics data offers a promising alternative to traditional black-box representation learning by separating the semantic concepts embedded in a biological process. We present CausCell, which incorporates the causal relationships among disentangled concepts within a diffusion model to perform disentanglement learning, with the aim of increasing the explainability, generalizability and controllability of single-cell data, including spatial and temporal omics data, relative to those of the existing black-box representation learning models. Two quantitative evaluation scenarios, i.e., disentanglement and reconstruction, are presented to conduct the first comprehensive single-cell disentanglement learning benchmark, which demonstrates that CausCell outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in both scenarios. Additionally, CausCell can implement controllable generation by intervening with the concepts of single-cell data when given a causal structure. It also has the potential to uncover biological insights by generating counterfactuals from small and noisy single-cell datasets.

Our desktop application MBCO PathNet allows for quick and easy integration and visualization of networks of functionally related pathways predicted from numerous gene and protein lists using the Molecular Biology of the Cell Ontology (MBCO) and other ontologies. Within networks of hierarchical parent-child relationships or functional relationships, pathways are visualized as pie charts where each slice represents a dataset that predicted that pathway. Sizes of pies and slices can be selected to represent statistical significance or other quantitative measures. In addition, MBCO PathNet can generate bar diagrams, heatmaps and timelines.
